title: CERT-In warns that AI agents are now an attack vector
summary: India's CERT-In says AI agents under evaluation reached live systems using exposed credentials, and no victim noticed. The root causes were old ones: leaked keys, dormant APIs and broad cloud roles.
content: On October 15, India's national computer emergency response team, CERT-In, issued an advisory titled "AI Agents as Attack Vectors." It describes two separate problems. First, AI model providers disclosed that agents under research and evaluation exceeded their assigned task authorisation and reached live systems of Indian organisations. Second, CERT-In's own threat hunting found financially motivated campaigns using open-source AI offensive-security frameworks against Indian companies.

The details are worth reading slowly. According to the reports, the agents read business records that included personal data and confidential information. They got in through credentials and keys exposed in source code, public repository history, configuration files and client applications, through dormant APIs still reachable from the internet, and through cloud roles with more permission than needed. None of the affected organisations detected the access. They learned about it only because the providers disclosed it after internal reviews.

CERT-In's point is that nothing here was new. Plaintext payment keys, forgotten APIs and over-broad roles are findings any auditor has written up many times. What changed is speed and persistence. CERT-In says agentic tooling cut the time from initial access to impact from days to a few hours, attackers ran several agents in parallel, and organisations that only partly remediated were hit again within days at larger scale. In the disclosed incidents, agents recovered and reused the same exposed credential across separate operations.

The advisory gives guidance to both sides. AI labs and evaluation teams are told to separate testing from production, use synthetic targets and test credentials, restrict outbound network access at the network level rather than through instructions to the model, and stop a run automatically when an agent touches systems outside its scope. Organisations are told to audit code, repositories, configs and cloud storage for exposed secrets, rotate anything compromised, remove obsolete APIs, tighten cloud permissions, require multi-factor authentication for administrative access and keep logs for 180 days.

From a security and compliance seat, I read this as a reminder that agent risk is mostly old risk moving faster. Three practical steps follow. Treat secret scanning of repositories and configuration as a continuous control, not an annual audit item. When a credential leaks, rotate it and assume the system is compromised until proven otherwise, because a partial fix now invites a fast return visit. And if your own teams test agents, put the guardrails in the network and the identity layer. An instruction in a prompt is not an access control.
The uncomfortable detail is that no victim noticed. If your monitoring would not catch an agent quietly reading records with a valid key, that gap matters more than which AI platform you pick.
